title: Ranking Is Not a Property: Tolerance Budget, Dispatch Boundaries, and the Cost of Admission
abstract: A kernel speedup is a point sample presented as a property: it does not say which shapes the advantage survives on, which reference realization scored the pass, or how much tolerance budget that reference already spends before a candidate is measured. We price all three on a DGX Spark (GB10, sm_120). With rho the reference's own consumption in multiples of the contract budget, an ordinary fp32 matmul reference grows in reduction depth without moving its pass verdict: 4/6 seeds pass at K=3608 and 2/6 at K=3632, no seed is monotone, and the fraction re-enters at K=3840. fp32 conv2d is a two-class dispatch surface over the tuple, not a depth function: a winograd engine at rho 10.195 with 0.52% of elements over budget and bit-identical output under every precision flag a user is told to set, versus TF32 tensor-op engines at rho 251.69 with 78.2% over budget, removed 99.9% by allow_tf32=False. At the official L1/40 LayerNorm shape the reference is anchor-clean on the benchmark's uniform input (rho 0.011) but reaches rho 2.529 with 19% of elements over budget at mean/std 1000, where a split-statistics candidate sits at 0.663 and still fails the candidate-versus-reference check. Admission is a binary whole-tensor check against the recorded reference, and is a class of its own, not implied by rho. Bulk classification (frac_over > 0.5) is 100% predictable from the engine class and does not transfer to admission, while the class itself is only 0.604 predictable against a 0.5625 majority from the four coordinates. Magnitude compresses onto derived coordinates (Spearman 0.986 with the class, 0.833 geometry-only) but admission does not. On 34 held-out shapes, reduction deliveries are admissible on 9 of 12 at 0.86% cost and conv on none.
